title: India's Services Engine Just Hit Its Slowest Speed in 17 Months — and Hiring Has Nearly Stalled
excerpt: The HSBC India Services PMI fell sharply to 57.4 in June as domestic demand weakened to its lowest in over two years, even as export orders offered a partial cushion
body:
India's services sector — the engine that drives more than half the economy's output — just recorded its weakest expansion in 17 months, raising fresh questions about the durability of the country's growth story even as Wall Street raises its GDP forecasts. For Non-Resident Indian (NRI) investors, this slowdown in a key economic pillar warrants close attention, as it could impact everything from investment returns to the broader economic sentiment back home.

The HSBC India Services Purchasing Managers' Index fell to 57.4 in June from 59.8 in May, according to data released on Friday by S&P Global. While any reading above 50 signals expansion, the magnitude of the drop — 2.4 points in a single month — marks the steepest deceleration since late 2024 and the lowest reading since January 2025.

"The loss of momentum points to more challenging market conditions and weaker demand, particularly at home," said Pranjul Bhandari, chief India economist at HSBC.

## Domestic Demand Is the Problem

The headline number masks a stark divergence. Domestic demand, which had been the services sector's primary growth engine, weakened sharply. New business — the PMI's key gauge of demand — rose at its slowest pace in more than two-and-a-half years, with firms reporting that challenging market conditions and reduced client interest stifled sales. This softening domestic demand could signal reduced consumer spending, a crucial factor for many businesses, including those that NRIs might have invested in or have family ties to.

Hiring, which had shown robust growth through April and May, nearly stalled. Only around one per cent of surveyed firms reported adding staff, with the rest finding that current payroll numbers were sufficient for weakening demand. The employment sub-index retreated to its weakest level of the year. A slowdown in job creation in the services sector, which is a major employer, could have implications for remittances and the economic stability of families back in India.



> **""The loss of momentum points to more challenging market conditions and weaker demand, particularly at home," said Pranjul Bhandari, chief India economist at HSBC."**


Business confidence also faded to a five-month low. Firms cited competition, difficult economic conditions and rupee depreciation as drags on sentiment — concerns that echo the broader caution among corporates about global trade uncertainty and financial market volatility.

## Exports Offer a Partial Offset

Not everything in the data was gloomy. International demand held up well, with new export orders growing at their fastest pace in three months. Firms reported improved demand from clients in Australia, Belgium, Canada, Germany, Malaysia, Nepal, Oman, Qatar, Singapore, the UAE and the United States. This resilience in external demand is particularly relevant for NRIs working in or investing in India's export-oriented service industries.


![Wall Street — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f5/Photos_NewYork1_032.jpg)


"External demand held up well as overseas sales stayed robust and growth reached a three-month high," Bhandari noted. For an economy that has been trying to diversify its services exports beyond traditional IT outsourcing — into consulting, healthcare, education and digital services — the export resilience is an encouraging signal.

Price pressures also eased. Input cost inflation dropped to a five-month low as electricity, food, fuel and transportation prices rose at a softer pace. Firms passed on less of that burden to clients, with the prices-charged sub-index falling to a seven-month low. The cooling inflation could give the Reserve Bank of India additional room to support growth if the domestic slowdown deepens.

## Manufacturing Is Softening Too

The services PMI reading arrived on the heels of Tuesday's manufacturing PMI, which also disappointed. Factory output expanded at its second-slowest pace since mid-2022, with the manufacturing PMI slipping to 54.2 in June from 55.0 in May. New orders, output and employment all softened.

The combined India Composite PMI — covering both services and manufacturing — slipped to its weakest level since March, painting a picture of broad-based private sector deceleration heading into the second quarter of fiscal year 2027. This broader slowdown across sectors suggests that the challenges are not isolated, potentially affecting a wider range of investment portfolios for NRIs.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

The timing of this slowdown is significant for overseas investors. Just this week, Wall Street firms including Bank of America and Goldman Sachs upgraded India's GDP growth forecast to 7 per cent, citing lower oil prices and the US-Iran peace dividend. Foreign portfolio investors, who had sold a cumulative ₹2.7 lakh crore of Indian equities in 2026, have begun to pare their selling — and inflows into US-listed India-focused ETFs turned positive last week for the first time in over a month.

But the PMI data introduces a counterweight. If services growth continues to decelerate, the earnings recovery that fund managers are counting on — analysts expect mid-teens profit growth in fiscal 2027 and 2028 — could prove elusive. The services sector accounts for more than 55 per cent of India's GDP and is the primary employer in the organised economy. A sustained hiring freeze in services would ripple through consumer spending, credit growth and, ultimately, corporate revenues. For NRI investors, this could mean a re-evaluation of growth-oriented investments, particularly in sectors heavily reliant on domestic consumption or employment.

For now, the market appears willing to look through the data. The Sensex climbed nearly 300 points on Friday, led by IT stocks buoyed by the weak US jobs report that took a Fed rate hike off the table. But the PMI's message is clear: India's macro tailwinds — falling oil, a stabilising rupee, fading geopolitical risk — may not be enough if the domestic demand engine sputters.

The next data point to watch is the first-quarter earnings season, which begins in earnest next week with TCS and Infosys. If the services slowdown is showing up in order books and deal pipelines, markets will notice, and NRI investors should be prepared to adjust their strategies accordingly.
